title: Is Goldman Sachs (GS) Primed for a Q1 Earnings Beat - Kavout | AI
content: Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) is set to announce its first-quarter 2026 earnings before market open on Monday, April 13, 2026, and Wall Street is bracing for a robust performance. The investment banking giant has a history of exceeding expectations, with an impressive average earnings surprise of 14.02% over the last four quarters. This consistent outperformance sets a high bar, yet current market dynamics suggest the firm is well-positioned to clear it once again. Analysts are forecasting a significant uplift, with consensus estimates for Q1 2026 revenue ranging from $16.66 billion to $17.40 billion, representing a projected 12.9% year-over-year increase. Earnings per share (EPS) are anticipated to be in the range of $16.41 to $16.86. These figures underscore a period of strong client activity and market volatility that Goldman Sachs has historically capitalized on, particularly within its Global Banking & Markets division. The current market environment, characterized by shifting expectations around artificial intelligence, persistent inflation concerns, and geopolitical tensions, has fueled volatility across asset classes. This backdrop creates fertile ground for Goldman's market-making and trading desks. While the broader M&A landscape remains somewhat subdued, the resurgence in initial public offerings (IPOs) and strong bond issuance volumes are expected to provide a significant tailwind to investment banking fees. However, it's not all smooth sailing. Goldman faces rising operating expenses due to ongoing investments in technology and strategic growth initiatives. The firm's ability to manage these costs while delivering top-line growth will be a critical focus for investors. Despite these headwinds, the overall sentiment remains cautiously optimistic, with the firm's strategic realignment towards a more diversified revenue base proving effective in a fractured global economy. Goldman Sachs' Q1 performance will largely hinge on the strength of its core operating segments, particularly Global Banking & Markets. This division, encompassing investment banking, equities, and fixed income, currencies, and commodities (FICC) trading, is expected to be the primary engine of revenue growth. Analysts project 'Net Revenues - Global Banking & Markets - Total' to reach approximately $12.65 billion, marking an 18.1% increase from the prior-year quarter. Within this segment, trading desks are anticipated to deliver exceptional results. High market volatility across equities, commodities, bonds, and foreign exchange, coupled with robust client activity, has created favorable conditions. In Q4 2025, the firm reported record equity trading revenue of $4.31 billion and a 12.5% rise in FICC revenue to $3.11 billion, and this momentum is expected to have carried into Q1 2026. The ability to monetize volatility remains a hallmark of Goldman's trading prowess. Investment Banking (IB) fees are also projected to see a substantial rebound, with consensus estimates at $2.6 billion, a 33.1% rise year-over-year. This resurgence is primarily driven by an impressive IPO market and solid global bond issuance volumes. While the M&A engine has sputtered due to regulatory scrutiny and geopolitical uncertainty, Goldman's leadership in equity capital markets and advisory services for strategic transformation deals has helped offset some of the broader slowdown. However, the stalling M&A landscape remains an "elephant in the room." While a handful of "megadeals" in technology and energy have kept some activity afloat, broader mid-market volume has plummeted. This creates pressure for Goldman to demonstrate the resilience of its fee-based revenue model even when one of its primary engines is idling. The firm's strategic pivot towards capital-light, fee-generating activities like IPO underwriting, rather than capital-intensive bridge financing for M&A, is a direct response to evolving market and regulatory conditions. Goldman Sachs' current valuation metrics present a mixed picture, reflecting both its strong operational performance and the inherent risks of the financial sector. The stock is currently trading at $907.80, with a market capitalization of $269.39 billion. Its trailing twelve-month (TTM) P/E ratio stands at 16.53, which is slightly above the industry average of 15.13x but below its 52-week high of $984.70. This suggests the market is pricing in continued growth, but perhaps with some caution. The price-to-book (P/B) ratio of 2.27 indicates that the market values Goldman Sachs at more than twice its book value per share of $399.65. While this can be a sign of strong asset quality and brand equity, it also highlights that the stock is not trading at a deep discount. The firm's debt-to-equity ratio of 4.88 is a point of consideration, reflecting the highly leveraged nature of investment banking, though this is typical for large financial institutions. Analyst sentiment for GS is generally positive, albeit with a "Hold" consensus rating from 55 analysts. Out of these, 22 recommend a "Buy," 30 suggest a "Hold," and only 3 advise "Sell." The median price target is $990.00, implying an upside of approximately 9% from the current price, with a high target of $1100.00. Recent rating changes from Evercore ISI Group and Jefferies both maintained "Outperform" and "Buy" ratings, respectively, on April 6, 2026, just days before the earnings release. Despite the positive outlook from many analysts, the stock's performance in Q1 2026 saw Goldman's shares lose 3.7%, while the broader industry declined by 8.6%. This relative outperformance, even in a down quarter, underscores the firm's resilience. However, the slight downward revision of 3.7% in the consensus EPS estimate over the past 30 days suggests some analysts have tempered their initial projections, making the actual earnings beat even more critical for investor confidence. The bull case for Goldman Sachs post-earnings hinges on several powerful tailwinds. First, the firm's ability to consistently beat earnings estimates, with an average surprise of 14.02%, suggests a strong operational execution that often exceeds conservative analyst models. If Q1 2026 continues this trend, it could provide a significant boost to investor confidence and the stock price. The projected 12.9% year-over-year revenue increase, driven by robust trading and ECM, indicates strong underlying business momentum. Furthermore, Goldman's strategic pivot towards a more diversified, fee-based revenue model, emphasizing Asset & Wealth Management, offers a more stable earnings base less susceptible to the boom-and-bust cycles of traditional investment banking. The firm's asset turnover of 0.07 and return on equity (ROE) of 13.8% demonstrate efficient capital deployment and strong profitability. Should geopolitical tensions de-escalate in the latter half of 2026, a massive backlog of "paused" M&A deals could unleash a record-breaking period, with Goldman perfectly positioned to capture this "snap-back" activity given its #1 ranking in deal volume. However, the bear case presents equally compelling arguments. The stalling M&A engine, a traditional stronghold for Goldman, remains a significant headwind. Regulatory scrutiny, particularly on "megadeals" in defense and energy, is causing "regulatory friction" and delaying transactions, forcing corporate boards to prioritize organic growth over acquisitions. This shift fundamentally alters the Wall Street landscape, and while Goldman is adapting, the long-term impact on its advisory revenue stream is uncertain. Rising operating expenses, fueled by investments in technology and growth initiatives, could compress margins if revenue growth doesn't keep pace. The firm's current ratio of 0.83 indicates a less liquid position than some peers, and its net debt/EBITDA of 18.53 highlights a substantial debt load relative to earnings. Moreover, insider trading activity shows a clear trend of net selling, with 133 sales and 0 purchases over the past 6 months, including significant sales from EVP John F.W. Rogers and CFO Denis P. Coleman totaling roughly $112 million. This insider behavior could signal a lack of conviction in the stock's near-term upside, despite the positive analyst outlook. For investors, Goldman Sachs' upcoming Q1 2026 earnings report represents a crucial inflection point. The firm's ability to navigate a complex macroeconomic environment, characterized by both high volatility and regulatory headwinds, will be under intense scrutiny. A strong beat, particularly in its Global Banking & Markets and Asset & Wealth Management divisions, could reinforce the narrative of a resilient, adaptable financial powerhouse. The market is currently pricing in a decent performance, but any significant deviation from analyst expectations could trigger a sharp reaction. Investors should pay close attention to management's commentary on the outlook for M&A activity, the sustainability of trading volumes, and the trajectory of operating expenses. The strategic pivot towards wealth and asset management, alongside its robust trading operations, is key to Goldman's long-term "durability" and less dependence on the cyclical nature of investment banking. Goldman's dividend yield of 1.80% and quarterly payout of $4.50 per share, with a payout ratio of 30.7%, offers a steady income stream, but capital appreciation will depend heavily on its ability to execute its strategy and capitalize on market opportunities. The firm's forward estimates for FY 2028 and FY 2029 revenue of $68.1 billion and $69.0 billion, respectively, and EPS of $71.36 and $75.79, suggest a positive long-term growth trajectory. Ultimately, Goldman Sachs remains a bellwether for the broader financial industry. Its Q1 results will not only reflect its own performance but also offer insights into the health of capital markets and the global economy. Investors should approach the earnings call with a balanced perspective, weighing the firm's proven ability to monetize volatility against the persistent challenges in certain core segments. Goldman Sachs is demonstrating remarkable resilience, leveraging its dominance in trading and capital markets to offset M&A headwinds. The upcoming earnings report will be a critical test of its strategic adaptability and ability to deliver value in a high-stakes environment. According to Woofun AI, David Solomon, Chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs (GS.US), has publicly voiced his support for the Digital Asset Market Clarification Act (CLARITY Act), a move that is extremely rare among leaders in traditional finance. Solomon acknowledged that the bill is far from perfect but emphasized that its core aim is to create a level playing field and enhance market stability, with the goal of establishing a regulatory framework for the crypto industry. On Wednesday, Republican senators in the U.S. Senate released the text of a bill, with its ethical‑conduct provisions becoming the focal point of political maneuvering. These provisions have sparked serious concerns among Democrats due to U.S. President Donald Trump's investments in the cryptocurrency sector. As of Thursday, the Senate leadership had not yet scheduled a specific vote. According to Woofun AI, the key variable in the current legislative process is the level of acceptance of the ethical provisions, which directly affects the feasibility of bipartisan cooperation and has brought the originally anticipated rapid progress to a standstill. Jamie Dimon, chairman of JPMorgan (JPM.US), expressed a markedly different view in an interview in May. He criticized the bill for allowing cryptocurrency firms to pay interest or yields on stablecoins while failing to grant them the same protective standards as traditional financial institutions. Dimon explicitly stated that such a double standard is something the banking system would never accept, arguing that it undermines the fairness of the financial system. This stance reflects the traditional banking sector's caution regarding the expansion of decentralized finance, and the fundamental divergence between the two sides over the regulatory rationale for stablecoins constitutes the primary obstacle to advancing the bill. Despite the bill's imminent vote, Republicans will need to secure support from some Democrats to reach the 60-vote threshold required for passage. Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren sharply criticized the bill, pointing out that it transfers law-enforcement responsibilities to the U.S. Department of Justice rather than state authorities, and even protects the president's financial interests in the cryptocurrency sector, thereby obstructing accountability for Trump. Warren argued that the bill fails to adequately safeguard investors, the financial system, and national security, and should never have been considered for enactment in the first place. One of the student leaders, Carter Ellington, 19, from Valdosta, did not go through BUILD as a freshman, but she has since participated in Southern Leaders, a multi-year student leadership program which, like BUILD, is coordinated through the university’s Office of Leadership and Community Engagement. She has also stepped forward in the community as a volunteer, such as with summer camps for foster children at 7th Mile Farm. So, Ellington was recruited to be a BUILD leader, and said she enjoyed working with the newer students and watching them grow some in just four days, or five if you count from their arrival on campus around midday Sunday. “I love volunteering and I thought I was just going to be volunteering and feeling that feeling, but actually watching them, the students, feel like they are making an impact and for one they’re being heard and seen and they’re doing something that makes other people feel heard and seen, that’s been so awesome to watch,” she said. BUILD stands for Building Undergraduate Involvement in Leadership Development, which may be one of those acronyms that led to a full name instead of the other way round. Incoming first-year students who participate arrive a full month before fall semester actually begins and pay a $200 fee to cover the cost of their lodging – in a temporary residence hall assignment – meals, transportation, equipment and leadership. The other student BUILD leader with Thursday’s group at the Food Bank, Jake Arispe, 21, from the Atlanta area, is also heading into his junior year. But BUILD leaders can be sophomores, juniors or seniors, and there were eight this year, guiding, assisting and to some extent counseling the incoming first-year student volunteers. In fact, Arispe was a BUILD volunteer the summer before his first year at Georgia Southern, and a BUILD leader going into his second year, as well as now, his third. “I had a great time my freshman year,” he said. “It definitely helped me get acclimated to campus, the community, and then also meet a bunch of different people, learned all about the community, the outreaches that different places do.” The volunteer work assignments typically last from 9 a.m. until noon. Other activities, and debriefing sessions in which volunteers and leaders talk about topics such as leadership and community involvement, occupy afternoons and evenings. The new students also get to know each other, and a little about campus and Statesboro. “I definitely felt more comfortable once I got to campus because of it,” Arispe said, recalling his freshman experience two years ago. Incidentally, Ellington is majoring in criminal justice as a pre-law student, but Arisbe majoring in sports medicine and finance. So it’s not like the student leaders are all planning to be counselors or work for some Chamber of Commerce. A variety of different academic interests was also evident in three young men, all 18 years old from various areas of Georgia, who appeared to be friends already. Miles Hill, from Austell, is an intended theater major. Tristan Clark, from Burke County, plans to major in criminal justice & criminology and to minor in cybersecurity. Myles Benjamin, from McDonough, intends on a geosciences major and hopes to become a meteorologist. Clark said the program was better than he expected when he signed up. “I think the amount of friends I’ve made this week is amazing” he said. “You know, I feel so close to them, even after just a week,” he said. One of his previous volunteer exploits of the week involved sorting shoes at a Christian ministry thrift shop. He and several of the other students said they also enjoyed some work they did at the Bulloch County Agricultural Complex. Benjamin noted that on one of the days, he had packed bags with T-shirts, grabbers and trash bags for Georgia Southern Eagles football players to use in a volunteer project of their own, cleaning up along a highway. Individual BUILD students went to four or five volunteer sites in the four work days. But altogether, the 50 freshman volunteers and eight student leaders did service work at 12 different places, reported Rachel Duvall, new this calendar year as director of the GS Office of Leadership and Community Engagement. Other jobsites included a couple of senior living facilities, Mattie Lively Elementary School, the United Way of Southeast Georgia and the university’s own Campus Community Garden. Besides getting down in the dirt gardening there, some students reported having pulled weeds and laid down mulch on the grounds of the Statesboro Family YMCA. “These incoming students really get exposed to the university and campus,” Duvall said. “So they learn some of our traditions, some of the things that make it meaningful to be a Georgia Southern Eagle, but also they are getting connected with the community. So hopefully, they’ll join us on service trips for the rest of the year.” Freshman Council within the Student Government Association is one of the opportunities some of these students may choose, she said. In addition to the SGA and Southern Leaders, the Office of Leadership and Community Engagement coordinates Serve 911, a program of weekly service trips. With those programs, students can continue to volunteer locally throughout their college years. But as a unique experience for incoming freshmen, BUILD also serves as a “little taste of independence” for some who have never been away from home before, Duvall noted. “So Day 1 they’re all nervous and they don’t want to talk to each other, and then by last (Wednesday) night they were hugging, dancing, having a party,” she said. “So it’s just nice to see them come out of their shells in a way that really prepares them for the larger college experience.” Many or all of the BUILD students will now go home before returning to campus for the real start of the semester. Operation Move-In Day is Aug. 14, for full-term classes to begin Aug. 19.

title: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon Reportedly Backs CLARITY Act In Split From JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon - TradingView
content: Goldman Sachs Group, Inc (GS) CEO David Solomon said on Thursday that he supported the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, commonly known as the CLARITY Act, a position that differs from other big bank CEOs, including JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon, who have opposed the bill. "I'm very supportive of moving the Clarity Act forward, so we can get some market structure in place and start to move the innovation process along," Solomon told POLITICO in an interview. Solomon refused to comment on the views of other bankers, but drew a clear line under Goldman's position. “We believe strongly that we need one system where everybody can participate,” he said, adding that Goldman Sachs’s position is that there will be other things that are “gonna have to happen as we go forward. But it’s a step in the right direction.” Unlike commercial lenders, investment banks like Goldman Sachs rely less on consumer deposits. Solomon said he has been focused on provisions that would allow “institutions that have been on the sidelines to participate more actively,” instead describing that as “the most important thing” in the bill at this stage. GS stock fell over 2% during midday trading. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around GS remained in the ‘neutral’ zone, while chatter around it stayed at ‘low’ levels over the past day. Solomon spoke just after Senate Republicans began circulating a new text of the bill before a possible floor vote next week. The new text followed an updated draft that Senator Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) unveiled on Wednesday, combining the separate bills previously passed by the Senate Banking and Agriculture Committees. A coalition of the industry’s most powerful groups, including the American Bankers Association (ABA), Bank Policy Institute, and Consumer Bankers Association, also warned on Wednesday that the bill’s stablecoin provision threatens “local lending that drives economic activity in the US at risk.” Solomon’s support puts him at odds with Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan & Chase (JPM), who had said the legislation would have exposed consumer banks to risk by giving crypto firms an unfair advantage with yield-based rewards on dollar-pegged stablecoins. Dimon also clashed publicly with Coinbase (COIN) CEO Brian Armstrong over the bill’s lobbying push in May. The bill's path forward remains uncertain, with unresolved fights over stablecoins, opposition from law enforcement groups, and the ethics language itself still in play ahead of any Senate vote. Warren Says Crypto Bill Could Never Be Enforced Against Trump Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) argued on Wednesday that the bill's enforcement was ineffective against President Trump himself. It will stop state attorneys general or anyone else from enforcing the law, leaving enforcement solely to Trump's own Attorney General. This meant it would cut off authority entirely once Trump left office, meaning no future Department of Justice (DOJ) could hold him accountable for violations committed while in power. Circle (CRCL) and Coinbase (COIN), the two firms that would benefit most from the CLARITY Act, were down over 5% and 2%, respectively, amid broader market weakness. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CRCL remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, while retail sentiment around COIN remained in the ‘bullish’ zone. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: By Light and Copper River Launch Copper Lights Joint Venture to Support Federal IT, Cyber, and Mission Requirements - markets.businessinsider.com

MCLEAN, Va., July  23, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- By Light Professional IT Services LLC and Copper River Government Solutions announced the launch of Copper Lights, a new joint venture formed to deliver advanced IT, cybersecurity, engineering, infrastructure and mission support solutions to federal customers, with an initial focus on Department of War and U.S. Space Force requirements. Copper Lights brings together By Light’s more than two decades of experience supporting defense and federal missions with Copper River GS’ high-performance technology solutions, engineering expertise and small business contracting capabilities. The joint venture was established to help agencies access an agile, mission-focused partner with the scale, technical depth and procurement flexibility needed to compete for and execute increasingly complex federal technology programs. “At By Light, we thrive on finding small businesses that complement our own capabilities and combining forces to solve some of the federal government’s most complex technology challenges,” said John Kilpatrick, vice president of space operations at By Light. “With their strength of experience in areas like network engineering and infrastructure, Copper River was a natural fit.” Copper Lights was formed under the U.S. Small Business Administration’s mentor-protégé program, with By Light serving as mentor and Copper River GS serving as protégé. Copper Lights combines By Light’ capabilities in cyber, communications, infrastructure, simulation and mission training with Copper River GS’ experience delivering cybersecurity, enterprise networks, mobility and end-to-end IT solutions. Copper River GS is part of the Copper River Family of Companies, which is owned by the Native Village of Eyak, a federally recognized Alaska Native Tribe. "Copper Lights gives our federal customers a single partner with deep technical expertise and the agility of a small business," said Ronald Allen, vice president for business development for Copper River's IT, Cyber and Professional Services group. "Copper River brings real domain expertise in cybersecurity, enterprise networking and end-to-end IT, and as a value-added reseller we can source and integrate the right commercial technologies to put that expertise to work. Paired with By Light's proven mission experience, that gives the Department of War and U.S. Space Force a faster, more flexible path to the solutions their missions demand." By Light Professional IT Services LLC, headquartered in McLean, Virginia, is a leading provider of advanced technology solutions delivering cyber and warfighter training platforms for Defense and National Security missions. The company operates two divisions—Cyber and Modeling, Simulation & Training—providing advanced cyber mission environments, synthetic training systems and AI-enabled live training that prepare forces for modern conflict. By combining mission expertise with cutting-edge commercial technologies and an expanding portfolio of advanced platforms, By Light helps defense organizations predict, prepare, and prevail with greater speed, realism, and operational advantage. For the latest information on By Light’s portfolio of products, solutions, and commercial capabilities, visit www.bylight.com. Copper River Family of Companies, headquartered in Chantilly, Virginia, is a Federally Recognized, Alaska Native, Tribal-Owned organization supporting critical government missions nationwide and abroad. Its family of operating companies delivers complementary capabilities spanning cybersecurity, network infrastructure, cloud and virtualization, digital transformation, managed and professional services, healthcare, construction, and maritime manufacturing. Owned by the Native Village of Eyak, Copper River combines mission-focused expertise with agile, customized solutions while generating economic and social benefits for the Tribe and its members. title: The Best Lexus 5.0 V8-Powered Sports Sedan Can Be Yours For The Same Price As A New ES Hybrid - CarBuzz
content: The BMW M5 is one of the most legendary performance cars ever produced, as it revolutionized the executive sports sedan market when it first hit the market in 1985. It has had to deal with a swarm of rivals trying to cash in on the lucrative sector since, though BMWs M Division has continually moved the bar ever higher to ensure the M5 retains its crown as the king of the mid-size premium sports sedan. This doesn't mean other rivals haven't gotten close, or surpassed the M5 in certain respects. The car in question went out of production in 2020, but this only means you can secure one for a lot less than its original MSRP on the used market. In fact, if you're in the market for a Lexus ES, but don't find it spicy enough, this might be the perfect solution. For most of its early history, Lexus tended to focus on the luxury aspect of its vehicles, rather than the sporting side. Some models, like the SC300 coupe, were a little more performative in nature, but they still angled more toward the smooth and silky side of the coin. Looking to expand its customer base, Lexus decided to establish its very own performance arm, called F, in 2006. The F department took a two-pronged approach to jazzing up Lexus' cars. It developed a range of F-Sport trim lines for lower-end models, which brought along mildly hot aesthetic and engineering enhancements, though the full-fat F cars were the ones for the true gearheads. These featured powerful naturally aspirated V8 engines, and focused chassis tuning that ensured they could take the fight to cars made by BMW's M division and Mercedes-Benz's AMG department. While the Lexus IS F was released in 2007 to take on the BMW M3 and Mercedes C63, it took until 2015 before Lexus unveiled a challenger to the likes of the M5. Wanting to be seen as a serious option alongside the mighty M5, Lexus pulled out all the stops to ensure the GS F could battle its German rival in its own backyard. Unfortunately, the GS F was short-lived, as it died along with the rest of the GS lineup after Lexus decided to retire the model in 2020. As a result, the only way to get one now is by purchasing a used example. Given its position as a range-topping executive sports sedan, the GS F wasn't exactly affordable when it was new. Even without any options selected, the GS F demanded over $85,000 from its buyer's bank account. It must be said that this was nearly $20,000 less than the M5's $102,000 price tag in 2020. As is usually the case with expensive vehicles that suffer steep depreciation, the value of the GS F have taken a tumble since then. The CarBuzz Marketplace values a solid 2020 example at $59,457. Earlier model-year cars can be had for significantly less. Bear in mind that the pre-2017 MY GS Fs didn't come with the marque's Adaptive Variable Suspension system, which is well worth having. It uses sensors to monitor the kind of road surface the GS F is traveling over, which can then select one of 30 different damper settings to suit. This ensures that whether the car is attacking a corner on a track or dealing with a rough road, which requires a smoother ride, it can change at a moment's notice. Prices for earlier models range vastly. A first model year with 100,000 miles on the clock can go for as little as $38,000, while a 2018 model with 30,000 miles of wear and tear will retail for $45,000. A good price to keep in mind is $50,000. For that, you get a car with the Adaptive Variable Suspension in one of the GS F's more sedate colors. For those looking for outright pace over a purely thrilling driving experience, it'll be difficult to see past the M5. The F90 version of the model introduced in 2018 comes with a 4.4-liter twin-turbo V8 packing 600 hp, which thoroughly decimates the 467 hp naturally aspirated V8 found under the hood of the GS F. As a result, while the M5 can hit 60 mph in a blazing 3.2 seconds, the GS F gets there in 4.5 seconds. Both come with automatic eight-speed transmissions. That said, the Lexus' V8 offers a much more exciting sound than the rather muted tones of the M5's twin-turbo unit, making it feel a little more alive when you hit the throttle. The GS F is also rear-wheel-drive as opposed to the all-wheel-drive BMW, which helps ensure the Lexus tips the scales at around 300 pounds less. For those looking to get their pulse racing, these rawer elements may prove more appealing than the efficiently quick M5. We wouldn't call one driving experience better than the other. They go about it in different ways as mentioned earlier. The F90 M5 has AWD because it needs it. 600 horses is just too much for the real world, especially in wet conditions. The GS F is a more balanced experience, and the 467 hp V8 never feels like more than the chassis (or driver) can cope with. You also can't beat the immediacy of a naturally aspirated V8 engine, which is all but gone from the new automotive market. In the case of the GS F, you're buying an experience that's no longer available. Even its little brother is no longer on sale, and as a result, its value have gone through the roof. While both share Lexus’ glorious, high-revving 5.0-liter naturally aspirated V8, the GS F stands out as a purpose-built performance machine, whereas the IS 500 is essentially a standard sport sedan with a huge engine shoehorned inside. As a true "F" model, the GS F gets extensive chassis bracing, massive six-piston Brembo brakes, and a sophisticated Torque Vectoring Differential for exceptional track handling. In contrast, the IS 500 carries base IS 350 brakes and a basic Torsen limited-slip differential. Add in aggressive sport seats, a roomier cabin, and superior cooling, and the GS F emerges as an uncompromised future classic. Aside from providing a thrilling drive, the GS F can also be trusted to get you to your next destination. While this shouldn't come as much of a surprise given Lexus' reputation for bulletproof reliability, as illustrated by the brand winning several JD Power dependability surveys in a row. RepairPal estimates the V8-powered beast should only cost around $499 a year to maintain. Its strong performance continues when you consider the National Highway Transport Safety Administration's records. The US Government-run department, which ensures every car sold in the US is safe, has yet to receive a single complaint regarding the car from an owner. One recall was filed for the vehicle by Lexus, which concerned the high-pressure fuel pump fitted to certain GS Fs made between 2016 and 2018. The component's cover could crack under load, which risked leading to a fire. All vehicles affected should already have had the fuel pump replacement carried out, but make sure when looking at a used example to confirm this. All in all, the GS F positions itself as a worthy alternative not just to the M5, but also to any new Lexus sedan. The 2026 Lexus IS starts at $46,895 and only offers an old-school V6. The all-new ES Hybrid starts at $51,095, and while it will undoubtedly be more modern, sophisticated, and frugal, all you'll get at this price point is a 244-hp four-cylinder hybrid. title: Four petrol bikes and one electric: Dalmatia, Bosnia, 3,000+ kilometers – How does that work? - THE PACK – Electric motorcycle news
content: First of all, a note of thanks: huge thanks to Manfred Janek for generously sharing this story, and to SteckerBiker for making the connection. These real-life, real-mileage travel reports are exactly the kind of content THE PACK wants more of: honest, funny, unglamorous-in-the-best-way accounts of what it’s actually like to ride electric, day after day, alongside people who didn’t necessarily choose to believe in it yet. (Story and photos originally by Manfred Janek for SteckerBiker. English retelling for THE PACK, based on the original German article >). Manfred Janek is now in his third season riding electric, and each year the concept wins him over a little more. His riding group runs a big annual tour, and in past years he’d simply retraced their petrol-bike routes afterward on his electric bike, solo – first a four-day loop through Bavaria and Austria, then a demanding 2,500 km, eight-day, roughly 30-pass run combining the Route des Grandes Alpes with Tuscany. For 2026, there was nothing left to retrace. So he decided to just join the group ride itself … on the electric bike. That meant matching pace with four full-size combustion machines: a BMW R1300 GS, a BMW R 1250 GS, a BMW F 750 GS, and a Ducati Multistrada V4S. Complicating things further, the whole route had already been planned by the R 1300 GS rider, hotels booked and daily stages fixed, back when everyone assumed Manfred would be riding his usual BMW K 1200 R. His first tentative suggestion of bringing the electric bike instead was flatly rejected. Only after checking that the route avoided highways and had just one stage over 400 km did the group come around. Manfred then built his own parallel plan: a charging point for every lunch stop, overnight charging at hotels, and – since the Großglockner pass was still on his personal electric-bike bucket list – a two-day solo extension after the group split off in Bosnia. He also had to switch hotels in Sarajevo when the original one couldn’t offer charging. That left him the outsider on three counts: electric instead of petrol, a solo cabin on the night train instead of sharing a four-berth compartment with the others, and a different hotel in Sarajevo. Not exactly the ingredients for a harmonious group photo. Manfred: “What you won’t find here, however, are elaborate descriptions of landscapes, old towns, coastal roads, or culinary highlights. The internet already has the hundredth travel report from the ten-thousandth GS rider. All I’ll say: they’re all lying. It’s even more beautiful.” The petrol group’s plan looked simple on paper: about 1,000 km from Graz to Dubrovnik, then another 1,000 km back north via Sarajevo. For Manfred, that’s where the real planning began – a second table tracking not just kilometers and riding time, but distances to the next charger. In the end, the plan held up well; the longest gap between chargers was about 225 km, comfortably within range. Day-to-day deviations came mostly from weather, ferries, road closures, and ordinary touring chaos – not from the electric bike. After the group returned through Bosnia, Manfred split off solo for another roughly 1,000 km home via Slovenia, the Großglockner, Mittersill, and several Alpine passes. Total distance: over 3,000 km. Manfred: “When planning, the others were mainly interested in two numbers: kilometers and travel time. I was interested in a third as well: “How far is the nearest power outlet?” That’s why, alongside the actual trip planning, I kept a second spreadsheet. While the petrol riders only knew where we’d sleep and drive, I also knew where my motorcycle and I would get our energy boost along the way.” On the road, the electric bike settled naturally into the ‘sweeper’ position at the back of the group – not because it was slow, but because the big adventure bikes, somewhat surprisingly, accelerated out of overtakes more gently than expected. When Manfred asked the R 1250 GS and Multistrada riders to give it more throttle on passes, the R 1250 GS rider insisted he already rode flat out – after which Manfred quietly backed off rather than risk a collision. He also highlights one underrated electric advantage: ultra-low-speed control. No clutch, no revs, no stalling – useful when the R 1300 GS routed the group onto increasingly rough, washed-out, muddy tracks better suited (on paper) to the ‘Adventure’ and ‘Enduro’ branding on the petrol bikes than to his own bike’s ‘Sports Road’ category. He couldn’t resist pointing that out to his companions; they were not amused. A city-traffic anecdote: stopped at lights beside the R 1300 GS in Sarajevo, its rider revved theatrically while waiting for green – only for the silent electric bike to pull away faster off the line, with no clutch or engine drama to manage. Another Sarajevo moment: to cut a 200-meter walk down to nothing, Manfred ‘pushed’ his powered-off-looking bike through a pedestrian zone at walking pace – technically legal, since a wheeled motorcycle counts as pedestrian traffic if no one can tell the motor is running. Overall, his companions can attest the electric bike never stood out dynamically – it stayed glued to the bike ahead even past 180 km/h. Its worst showing, ironically, came when Manfred led at the front through Bosnia and refused to exceed speed limits by more than 20 km/h – much to the group’s dismay. The widespread assumption before the trip – that petrol and electric bikes can’t tour together because the group will constantly be waiting on the electric one – turned out, in Manfred’s words, to be complete nonsense. The key factor: his bike started every morning full, while the petrol group was still checking tire pressure and weather apps over breakfast. Three to four hours of riding later, hunger stops did the charging for him; often a partial top-up during lunch was enough, and some days needed no charging stop at all. His bike supports three charging types – up to 12.3 kW via Type 2, up to 7 kW via three-phase power, and up to 3.3 kW via a standard household socket – used respectively on the road, for fun/emergency top-ups, and overnight at hotels. By the end, Manfred reckons he spent about as much time waiting for petrol riders at gas stations as they spent waiting for him at chargers. Manfred had never quite been happy with the stock Pirelli tires on his electric bike – wear was steep on the 2025 tour – so he fitted fresh Metzelers before this trip. Wear turned out excellent (only about 1.5 mm lost over 3,000+ km), but partway through Bosnia the bike started feeling odd in corners. When the group’s most vocal electric-bike skeptic, the R 1250 GS rider, borrowed it for a test ride, his verdict was blunt: great motor, terrible chassis, wobbling over bumps in lean – he’d never buy one. The real cause, discovered the next morning: a rear tire pressure of roughly 1 bar (practically flat), caused by a three-centimeter nail picked up somewhere in Dubrovnik. A Sarajevo tire shop fixed it in minutes for ten euros – plug in, air up, done – quietly clearing both the tires and the chassis of blame, and leaving Manfred crediting his small battery-powered air pump as the unsung hero of the trip. Hotels were consistently helpful about charging, most not even asking for payment (Manfred insisted on a flat 5-euro fee per night regardless). His one real complaint: charging fan noise – his “No Noise” marketed electric bike was louder overnight than all four petrol bikes combined, running its cooling fan continuously while charging. He asks manufacturers directly to fix this. Other asides: a plea to petrol riders to think about people standing behind them when they start a cold engine (especially night-train staff working around the bikes), and a tongue-in-cheek warning to Balkan snakes to watch for the Ducati Multistrada before crossing the road. A telling comparison: his electric bike used under 9 kWh per 100 km – roughly the energy content of one liter of gasoline – while the petrol bikes burned at least four liters per 100 km covering the same roads, speeds, and corners. He notes that the extra energy the four petrol bikes burned over the ~2,200 km group route could heat his daughter’s modern heat-pump house for half a winter. He closes with praise for the R 1300 GS rider’s hotel picks, especially two four-star, motorcycle-friendly properties in Sarajevo and Vransko, and a final charging/coffee stop at the R 1300 GS and F 750 GS riders’ home before the last 100 km. Asked for their verdict, the group was generally positive but flagged real trade-offs: “In the end, the charging stops didn’t slow us down because during shared breaks, we often used the available charging options. That way, we could usually continue riding together. However, the effort required to plan charging stops, search for alternatives if stations were occupied, and the limited ability to take spontaneous detours would personally take away a lot of the fun of a motorcycle trip for me.” “Ultimately, electric mobility always comes down to range. Many current models are too limited in this regard and are better suited for regional use. Your Zero really impressed me with its range of between 200–250 km. However, this requires a disciplined riding style, always keeping an eye on the remaining range. For me, riding a motorcycle is primarily an emotional experience where I want to be able to decide at any moment whether to speed up, cruise, extend the route, or take a shortcut. With the constant need to search for the next charging station, this spontaneity is partly lost, especially if the stations are occupied or even out of order.” “The only disadvantage for me personally would be the lack of spontaneity, which is a big part of what makes motorcycle riding so special. As long as you stick to the planned route with charging options, it surprisingly didn’t bother me much. I had expected that we would almost always have to split up during the midday break due to charging times. In the end, however, the lunch or sightseeing break was often long enough to fully charge the Zero so that it could reach the next destination. What did impress me was how quickly and directly the Zero puts its torque down the first time it overtakes you – you see how fast it shrinks into the distance, and it suddenly makes sense why someone would want to ride one.” “I never would have thought that riding style (speed, route planning) would have such a significant impact on range. But I also never would have thought that it would end up being so irrelevant: Even if we couldn’t ride together the entire day due to charging stops or range issues, we still almost always arrived at our destination at the same time.” Manfred didn’t expect a mixed-fleet tour through Dalmatia and Bosnia – regions with charging infrastructure still well behind Central Europe – to go this smoothly, especially since the entire route was planned for and by petrol bikes, with charging having to adapt around it rather than the reverse. The few tight moments came down to circumstances (or, in Knin, rider error) rather than any real limitation of the bike. His conclusion: petrol and electric motorcycles touring together already works far better than most riders would assume – the real differences show up in break planning, not in the riding itself. He closes half-jokingly asking readers not to rush out and buy electric bikes just yet, since being a small minority is exactly why hotels and chargers were so consistently available – a fleet of several electric bikes, or ones dependent solely on DC fast charging, would likely have forced real route changes. For this trip, though: the route worked, the team worked, the infrastructure was enough, and so was the bike.
